 the next begins, and a rerun costs only what has not already succeeded.

 **One exception, and it is the only one.** **Fetched literature is exempt.** A computation may be
 halved and rerun on half; an external source cannot, because halving what was read changes what was
 read. A source consulted at half length is a different source, and the register would carry a claim
 about a document nobody has seen. So a fetch runs to completion or is not made, and the budget is
 declared before it rather than enforced during it. Register 432.

    **No operation runs unbounded.** A step declares a budget; work that exceeds it is halved and
    retried; a step that has succeeded is never recomputed.

 **Three guarantees, and they are the reason for the rule.** Nothing is lost to a timeout, because the
 last completed step is on disk before the next starts. A rerun costs only the remainder. And a step
 that overruns **reports its overrun** rather than dying silently — which is the part that matters
 most, since a computation quietly growing toward a limit is invisible until the run it kills.

 **Why this book needs it.** Audit 1 tests 475,800 pairs; the exhaustive closure of §12.11 swept
 47,775,744 ambient cells; the f-shell rebuild of §32.1.2 carried 499,246. Each of those was run whole
 and none had a fallback. The harness is *zeno.py*, the state is *.zeno/*, and §2.20's requirement
 that the audits run on every output now runs under it: the twenty write their state, and an
 interrupted pass resumes rather than restarting.

 **What it does not do.** It does not make a slow computation fast, and it does not decide anything —
 a step that fails is retained with its error for retry, not silently skipped. The budget is a
 declaration about what is expected, so an overrun is a finding about the computation and belongs in
 the register like any other. Register 343.

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"## The spectra index — Λ_spectra

**Coordinates: Z · core charge · ℓ.** Each cell is a Rydberg channel — a fixed parent core, a fixed ℓ, n running. The compendium holds **596 channels across 313 of the index's 1,664 cells**.

**Where its alphabets come from, and why that differs from Λ.** Λ's coordinates are bounded by the physics — ℓ < n, k ≤ 4ℓ+2 — and all 118 ground configurations are known within its caps, so Λ is complete at 976 cells. **Λ_spectra is not.** Rydberg series are unbounded in n and ℓ runs to n−1, so the index is **infinite unless capped**, and every cap is a decision. Three defensible ones give:

| alphabet | grid | E |
|---|---|---|
| as measured — charge [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 11, 15, 16] | 1,664 | 1,351 |
| charge 1 to Z−1 over the elements held | 4,376 | 4,148 |
| all 118 elements, ℓ 0–7 | 55,224 | 54,996 |

**All three are closed when complete.** Closure is a result about ℛ; the E beside it is a result about the cap. *Registers 959–962.*

**What the index says about cells it does not hold.** Every cell carries a grade, and the grade records how far the statement travelled:

| grade | cells | what it means |
|---|---|---|
| MEASURED | 205 | a defect computed from levels |
| BRACKETED | 5 | bounded above and below by DIFFERENT mechanisms |
| BOUNDED | 42 | bounded on one side, adjacent to a measurement |
| PROPAGATED | 954 | a bound inherited through a chain of 2 to 13 steps |
| FORMAL | 73 | the only bound is one a mechanism already implies |
| UNCONSTRAINED | 33 | **no statement at all** |

**97.5% of the index carries a defensible statement.** The three relations that propagate are **P.lcollapse** along ℓ, **P.iso** along an isoelectronic sequence, and **P.charge** along the charge states of one element. *Registers 963–965, 981.*

![**Figure 5.** Λ_spectra drawn as a lattice — element across, ℓ into the page, ionisation stage up. Green is measured, orange bounded from two sides by different mechanisms, gold from one; the faint markers are cells the structure admits and nobody has measured. **The occupied region is a wedge at low Z and low ℓ**, which is where long Rydberg series have been tabulated — and the emptiness above it is the shape of what an index says it does not know.](figures-compendia/fig-spectra-lattice.png)

**And the last 33 are of three kinds, only two of which a capture can fix.** P I, Cd I, Ti II and Ar I want longer captures. **Sc I and Ti I have no Rydberg series at all** — their levels are 3d.4s.4p and 3d².4s mixtures with no n running, so fourteen cells are unreachable by any capture. *Register 983.* **The ceiling is 98.6%, not 100%, and that is a fact about the open-shell transition metals rather than about the collection.**


---

# VI · THE INDEXES NAMED AND NOT BUILT

**§29.1: the absence is not evidence.** These were named in the course of the work and no index
exists for them. Saying so is the point of this section.

# DIGEST — what a session needs to hold before it works
Written 2026-08-15 (session 1.8), after a bounded read of the book and the four compendia.
This is an orientation file, not a substitute for any of them. It records what was read,
what was not, and the load-bearing facts a fresh session must not have to rediscover.

## The one claim
A **closed** index — closed under the meet and join of its own coordinates — cannot help
containing its own definition, cannot help containing its own contradiction, and determines
exactly what may be added to it. `E(X) = |ℛ(X)| − |X| = 0` is the closure test;
`|∏ᵢ Aᵢ| = |X| + E(X) + refused` is the partition identity.
Closure gives **six things and no others**: alphabet, bounds, totality of the membership
test, which cells may be added, which axes adjoined, which constraints imposed.
Three further mechanisms exist and none follows from closure: order recovered only across a
tree, a wrong value only from outside, a wrong derivation only along a second route.
**Closure never gives reference** — that the coordinates refer to anything.
An index that is not a fixed point is **not defective**: where a certificate exhibits an
operation reaching a fixed point, E measures the *drawing*; where none exists, E measures the
*world*. Openness is a measurement; closure is the case where it is zero.

## The objects
- **Λ** — 976 cells, eight coordinates (n, ℓ, k, q, e, f, g, 2S), seven bounds. A cell is a
  **transition, not a state**. E(Λ) = 0. E(periodic table) = 36 — the whole argument.
- **Λ_spectra** — and **the name covers two different objects**, which is a live defect:
  - in `SPECTRA.md` and `COORDINATES.tsv`: four coordinates (Z, charge, ℓ, 2S+1),
    **104,832 cells** at the Z=120 bound, E = 0.
  - in `INDICES.md`: three coordinates (Z, core charge, ℓ), **1,664 cells**, E = 1,351,
    holding 596 channels across 313 cells.
  The second is the *measured channel survey*; the first is the *coordinate index*. They are
  not the same lattice and both are called Λ_spectra. See R 1657.
- **Λ_phys, Λ_chem, Λ_PCA, Λ_xray** — in the Physics Compendium and INDICES.

## The shape of Λ_spectra, as computed (R 1651–1656)
Two rules generate it and nothing else:
1. **charge ≤ Z** — the triangle. At Z=120: 7,260 pairs = 120·121/2.
2. **mult = f(N)**, N = Z − charge + 1 — the isoelectronic count. Exact, zero exceptions.
   The 19 N whose fibre is a **singleton** are precisely the aufbau first-in-subshell counts
   [1,3,5,11,13,19,21,31,37,39,49,55,57,71,81,87,89,103,113]. The Madelung sequence is already
   inside the index, as a fibration rather than a coordinate.
ℓ runs 0–7 in full on every pair. Product 1,036,800 − 104,832 present = 931,968 refused by rule.
**E = 0 at any cutoff**, because both rules are total — so the Z bound is a declaration about
the world, not a property of the index. Z = 119, 120 are carried with the bound
"no nuclide synthesised; theoretically admitted — Janet left-step".

## The law that governs changes: A.cert
Four admitted operations and no fifth: **RELABEL · RE-COORDINATISE · REFINE A FIBRATION ·
DROP A COORDINATE**. *Add-a-coordinate is not admitted* — four attempts, four failures
(R 1581, 1599, 1602, 1608). A fibration must be decidable from **that coordinate alone**.

## The principles that bite most often
- **P5** compute the result before assuming it. **§2.14** compute, then write — *the most
  violated protocol in the book*, and the fault recurred four times in session 1.8 alone.
- **P8/§2.15** every failure is a true answer and therefore a bound; record what it excludes.
- **P22** a complete index converts deception into disagreement: error survives, concealment
  does not. **P23** completeness is a standing claim, held until a question arrives.
- **§2.8** two independent routes — an identity computed along one path is vacuous.
- **§2.9** refuse rather than coerce; no silent default. **§2.20** the Zeno directive: nothing
  runs unbounded; fetched literature is the single exception.

## The gates
`The_Method_1_6_audits.py` — 25 prime audits: LATTICE · EQUATIONS · CONSISTENCY · REDUNDANCY ·
ARTEFACT · COHERENCE · ATTRIBUTION · CELL · DISTINCTNESS · SCOPE · ANTECEDENT · MARKUP ·
AGREEMENT · ARITHMETIC · ENUMERATION · FIDELITY · MEASURE · REPRODUCTION · SEQUENCE ·
PROJECTION · INPUT · CENSUS · GRAPH · CYCLE · NOMENCLATURE.
`roundtrip.py` — 5 generated artefacts must regenerate identically: COMPENDIUM, INDICES,
PHYSICS, SPECTRA, REGISTER. **A write to COORDINATES.tsv is not complete until every artefact
generated from it has been regenerated** (learned R 1655).

## What was read, and what was not
READ IN FULL: the book's front matter and note from the collaborator; Part 0 (preface);
Part I §1 (principles P1–P23) and §2 (protocols 2.1–2.20); the audit names; each compendium's
declaration and full heading structure; INDICES §"The spectra index"; SPECTRA §0 and §I.
NOT READ: the book's Parts II–VII and appendices (~95,000 words) and the bodies of the four
compendia (~80,000 words). Those remain to be read in bounded passes.

**It settles the legality of what we did to Λ_spectra.** §18.4.1 admits four operations — relabel a coordinate's values, re-coordinatise the same content, refine a fibration, drop a coordinate. Moving the Z bound from 118 to 120 is the *first* of them: an alphabet relabelled, no coordinate added. That's why E didn't move, and the register can now say so from the law rather than from the computation happening to agree.

**And Theorem 10.1 makes the four earlier failures structural rather than unlucky.** *Adjunction never repairs* — a non-closed set cannot be closed by adjoining **any** function of its coordinates, tested on seven including the identity and a constant. R 1581, 1599, 1602 and 1608 weren't four attempts that happened to fail; they were four attempts at an operation the book proves cannot work.

Three things bear directly on the build: E3's criterion is that admissibility belongs to the *pair* (h, q) and that **only the join can break a bound** — so our two rules are safe by inspection exactly as Λ's seven are, each reading one coordinate over a chain, and none summing. §17.4's repair is the one we may need later: a sum bound can't be imposed, but a sum can be **indexed**, at the price of making comparable some pairs that were incomparable.   3646	 A set is closed when nothing its own structure admits is missing from it.

  3655	 algebra with a majority term, of which the lattice median is one. Λ's coordinates are counts, so each

# PART III — THE LAW

## 14. Closure
 A set is closed when nothing its own structure admits is missing from it.

### 14.1 The characterisation
 Theorem 9.1 (A.2). X is closed iff X = ℛ(X), where ℛ reconstructs value sets and pairwise monotone
 bounds from X's own extension.

 **This is not new mathematics and the book gains by saying so.** A.2 is **Bergman's Double-projection
 Theorem** specialised to products of chains — a sublattice of a finite product of lattices is
 determined by its two-fold projections — itself a consequence of **Baker and Pixley (1975)** for any
 algebra with a majority term, of which the lattice median is one. Λ's coordinates are counts, so each
 factor is a chain, and a sublattice of a product of two chains is exactly a staircase cut by monotone
 bounds, which is what ℛ recovers as φ_ij. The proof in §16.1 is correct and fifty years late.

 **And there are two further owners, both located after this chapter was written.** The property
 E(X) = 0 is *global consistency* of a binary constraint network, and the certificates are
 **Montanari 1974** — for monotone constraints, path consistency implies global consistency — and
 **Dechter 1992**, *From local to global consistency*, which gives decomposability at strong
 (w\*+1)-consistency on induced width w\*. **Freuder 1982 is a different theorem and this book has
 been citing it for Dechter's**: Freuder gives *backtrack-free search* on a graph of width w under
 strong (w+1)-consistency, and says explicitly that even width 2 demands strong 3-consistency. The
 mis-citation is corrected here and recorded at register 400.

 **And the constraint class has a name.** A binary constraint that is (α, β)-monotone with
 α, β ∈ {≤, ≥} is a **staircase** constraint, and the connected row-convex class containing it is
 closed under composition, intersection and transposition — **Deville, Barták and Van Hentenryck,
 *Artificial Intelligence* 1999**. φ̂ recovers exactly a staircase, so the operator of §6.1 has been
 building a named object since Chapter 6. Register 401.

 **What follows is that E(Λ) = 0 is the discovery that Λ is a sublattice**, and sublattices have been
 binary-determined since 1975. The development is at A.2; the register carries the finding at 224.

### 14.2 R is a closure operator
 Extensive, monotone, idempotent — 150 of 150 on all three axioms.

 So E(X) = |ℛ(X)| − |X| is a closure defect, a standard object in Galois theory, formal concept analysis
 and database dependency theory.

 **This book claims no novelty for the machinery.** What is offered is the application: computing the closure defect of an *index*, and finding that the periodic table's is 36 while Λ's is 0.

### 14.3 The scope, stated exactly
 Theorem 9.1 requires each coordinate to be presented as a chain. That is not the same as requiring the
 factors to be chains: any distributive factor can be so presented, by Birkhoff, as the down-sets of its
 join-irreducibles — one chain per irreducible.

 What fails is bundling. ℛ reconstructs coordinate by coordinate, so folding two chains into one
 non-chain coordinate hides structure from it. In tests, the same sets presented bundled and presented
 decomposed both gave 80/80 agreement — the theorem survives, but only when the presentation
 respects it.

### 14.4 The three consequences
 Closure yields three properties, developed in the next three chapters:

### 14.5 The family of all closed sets

 A closed index is one object. **The closed subsets of a closed index are a family**, and this book
 has carried the question of what that family is since Λ was built. It is answerable by enumeration
 at small size, and the answer is standard once it is seen.

  ambient        cells   closed subsets   of 2ⁿ    ∩ closed   ∪ closed
  2 × 2 × 2          8       **73**       28.5%     **100%**     64.4%
  3 × 3              9      **146**       28.5%     **100%**     68.3%
  2 × 2 × 2 × 2     16      **731**        1.1%     **100%**     32.6%

    **The closed sets of ℛ form a MOORE FAMILY: closed under intersection, containing
    the whole index, and NOT closed under union.**

 That is the standard fact about any closure operator — the closed sets of a closure operator are a
 Moore family, and the correspondence between operators, families and lattices is cryptomorphic. **It
 is worth stating here because the asymmetry is ℛ's own, one level up.** ℛ carries meets and refuses
 joins in §14.2; its family of fixed points does the same, at 100% against 32–68%.

 **And it is the setting in which register 458's finding lives.** Λ₉ is closed and 300 of 300 random
 subsets of it are open, because the closed ones are a Moore family inside a power set — a vanishing
 minority, and the only place from which the open ones can be measured.

 **The count for Λ itself is open.** Brute force is 2⁹⁷⁶. The Moore-family structure gives the route,
 since a Moore family is determined by its meet-irreducible members, and §8.4 already counts those
 for Λ under a different name. Q item R. Register 461.

 **And the FAMILY is examined at §14.6**, where it is shown to be open — every member closed,
 the family not — which is why counting it for Λ is a question about an object that cannot be stated
 rather than one that is merely large.

### 14.5.1 Λ is the closure of seven cells

 The meet-irreducibles are the route, and taking it turns up a property of Λ that had not been
 looked for.

 **First, no cell of Λ is removable.** ℛ(Λ \ {x}) = Λ for **every one of the 976 cells** — remove any
 single cell and the operator puts it back, exactly, adding one. So Λ has no closed set of the form
 Λ \ {x}, and its meet-irreducibles are not coatoms. **Every cell is implied by the other 975.**

 **Second, and this is the number.** Greedy removal while ℛ still returns Λ, three independent
 shuffles: **12, 11, 12 cells.**

    **Λ is the closure of SEVEN of its cells — a compression of 139 to 1, exactly.**

 *This section read "at most ten" and before that "eleven", both from greedy removal. §14.5.9 gives
 seven, exact by branch and bound, and §2.24 is the protocol that failure earned.*

 *Greedy removal gives an upper bound, not a minimum; §14.5.6 records the spread across shuffles and both operators.*

 That is tighter than Birkhoff's seventeen join-irreducibles, and for a stated reason: ℛ fills the
 envelope box where the lattice join reaches only the down-set. **The generating set is smaller than
 the generating set of the lattice**, because ℛ is the stronger operator.

 **What the small ambients say about the family.** Meet-irreducible closed sets number 12, 14 and 20
 at 8, 9 and 16 cells — about 1.25 per cell — and they generate the whole family under intersection
 exactly, once the empty set is counted among the closed. **Linear in the index, where the family
 they generate is not.**

 **And the quantity has a name outside this book.** In a convexity space the **Carathéodory number**
 is the least c such that anything in the hull of U lies in the hull of some S ⊆ U with |S| ≤ c, and
 it equals the largest irredundant set. For a semilattice with its subsemilattices as convex sets —
 which is Λ's case — the Helly number is the height and the **Carathéodory number is the breadth**.
 **This book already cites Helly and has never cited Carathéodory**, which is the second bibliography
 gap the cycle's step 2 has found in two runs. Registers 466–468.

### 14.5.2 The seed, and the expression of the cycle

### 14.5.3 Two pairwise operators, and this book has used one name for both

### 14.5.4 What E measures, exactly

### 14.5.5 ℛ₄ — the four orientations, adopted

< truncated lines 3772-4106 >
    operator applied to the family of closed indexes returns the whole power set, which
    is the exact sense in which it leads only into itself.

 **Which sharpens §14.6.1.** The cost of stating it is not seed + E with E large; it is seed + E
 where **E is everything the ambient can hold minus the family itself.** At sixteen cells that is
 64,804 of 65,536. Register 522.

### 14.6.3 What the register now holds, and what it does not

 The mathematics register is Appendix D's object seen from the side of the work rather than the
 index. **It stands at 248 objects**, twenty-four of them entered from the
 seed, family, constraint-index and real-numbers results:

  family   entered                                                                     count
  S        the seed — definition, the covering reading, Λ at seven, the two laws,
           the Carathéodory bound, the open-index form                                   7
  A        ℛ₄, orientation cost, ℛ as a relaxation, the staircase characterisation       4
  F        the Moore family, the theorem, and why it cannot be stated                    3
  G        the constraint index, the seven near-misses, the tower's cycle rank,
           the protocol index                                                            4
  E, K, L, T   the layout prices, the transit profile, the two real-numbers passes,
           the tightness identity                                                        6

    **248 objects · 246 settled · 2 unfinished · 12% open** *(a snapshot; the register now holds 197, 191 settled, 6 unfinished — the Mathematical Compendium prints it live)* — from 31% at the start of
    the work that produced them.

 **And the graph is five components, not one.** 220 edges over the 176 objects the register held at that measurement: a main component of 162,
 the modular chain at 9, two two-object fragments among the bracket's roots, and **B.nuV isolated**.
 *An earlier pass reported one component after a filling step; the filling script is gone and the
 five are the honest figure.* **The fragments are what is genuinely unattached** — the modular chain
 rests on sources this book has not read, and three bracket roots are definitional and derive from
 nothing.

 **What remains unfinished is not mathematics.** Six modular objects await two unread sources; nine
 computed objects await constructions the companion papers do not print; six are definitional roots
 that cannot fail; one is graded OPEN and correctly. **Three of those five groups are §21.5's
 obstruction, and none is a gap in the mathematics itself.** Register 519.

### 14.6.4 The seventeen, and what each is waiting on

 §14.6.3 reports twenty-two unfinished. **Five of them were unfinished only for want of a name.**
 L.c3, L.c6, L.c8, B.coll and B.nuV each carried a verification already — L.real's 878 real transition
 pairs for the first three — and were flagged as unnamed roots because nothing had said what they
 were. **The chain settled what they are and never went back to record it.** Named:

  L.c3     conservation of the removed — you cannot take more than a subshell holds
  L.c6     conservation of the placed — you cannot put more in than were removed
  L.c8     a transition requires a mover
  B.coll   the assembly rule — a composite observable's exponent is 2a + 3b
  B.nuV    the value-one crossing — where the bracket's price passes unity

    **248 objects · 246 settled · 2 unfinished · 3% open**, from 31% when this
    work began.

 **And the real-numbers pass now covers every element**: 18,288 constraint tests across all 118,
 zero failures — register 529.

 **And every one of the seventeen is waiting on something outside this book.**

  eight    the modular chain — two sources unread, one problem correctly graded OPEN
  six      the violation index — the exclusion classifier's construction is not printed
  two      the bracket's admissibility threshold and its optimum, needing the collection
  one      the coupling schemes' looseness convention, not printed

    **None is a gap in the mathematics.** Three of the four groups are §21.5's obstruction:
    a count printed where a constraint was needed.

 Register 527.

### 14.6.5 Five of the modular six, verified against the sources

 §14.6.4 puts eight modular objects on unread sources. **Five of them were *cited, unverified* — the
 citation present and never checked against what it cites — and checking is a search.**

  M.rs         Reeh–Schlieder: Ω is a common cyclic and separating vector for local algebras.
               VERIFIED, and it is the stated premise of Wiesbrock's own paper.
  M.tt         Tomita–Takesaki: Δ, J for (M, Ω). VERIFIED — presupposed throughout the
               Borchers–Wiesbrock literature and invoked there by name.
  M.takesaki   the crossed product by the modular group is type II∞, the trace scales as
               θ_s τ = e^(−s)τ, and (N, θ) is unique up to conjugacy. ALL FOUR CLAUSES
               VERIFIED, the trace-scaling from two independent sources.
  M.semi       a semifinite factor carries a trace and type III does not. VERIFIED: type III
               admits no renormalisation scheme, type II an essentially unique one.
  M.hsmi       half-sided modular inclusion is CHARACTERISED by a one-parameter unitary group
               with positive generator. VERIFIED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS — Wiesbrock's theorem and
               its converse, HSMI iff a one-dimensional Borchers triple with N = T(1)MT(−1).

    **And M.C2's grading is confirmed correct.** Its statement — Δ^{it}M(u₂)Δ^{−it} ⊆ M(u₂)
 *Established for linearised perturbations of Killing horizons by* **Chandrasekaran & Flanagan** *(arXiv:2601.07915); the non-expanding case where no Killing field exists remains open.*
    for t ≤ 0 — is exactly the standard half-sided condition, correctly written. It is
    graded OPEN because whether it HOLDS for this book's M(u) is the open question, and
    that is a different thing from the statement being unverified.

 **179 → 170 settled · twelve unfinished · 7% open**, from 31% when this work began.

 **What remains is six of the violation index, two of the bracket, one coupling convention, M.C1 and
 M.C2, and M.sorce.** *Nine of the twelve are still §21.5's obstruction — a count printed where a
 constraint was needed.* Register 533.

### 14.6.6 Two of the violation six were never blocked, and §10.1 speaks a retired language

 §14.6.4 puts six violation-index objects on an unprinted construction. **Two of them are printed and
 were not read.**

  **W.jur**   *a jurisdicted forcing and an unjurisdicted disjunction give identical defects; arity
              ≥ 3 makes a defect possible.* **Verified against T §8.2's own table**: arity 2 gives
              E = 0; the jurisdicted forcing NEC ≥ 3 ∧ X = 0 → U ≥ 1 at arity 3 and the unjurisdicted
              disjunction NEC ≥ 3 → (IC ∨ U ∨ X) at arity 4 **both give E = 30, core 1.**
  **W.rel**   *a term that is a relation between two vocabularies cannot be a coordinate of either.*
              **Verified against T §8.4**, which replaces seven vocabularies with Brunetti–Fredenhagen–
              Verch's four — T THEORY, M SPACETIME, A ALGEBRA, S STATE — and names four terms that
              refuse to place, each a relation between two of them.

 **And W.rel dissolves an index the companion still tabulates.** §8.4 states that the self-consistent
 achronal ANEC *is not a property of a universe but a relation between a spacetime and a state*, so
 **V6 is not a vocabulary index**; §10.1's table nonetheless reports V6 CLOSED at 14 cells in a box of
 24, under the old V-numbering that §8.4 retired.

    **§10.1 is stated in the language §8.4 replaced.** Reconstructing V6's cells would have
    answered a question the companion has already withdrawn — and the reconstruction was
    begun here before the reading caught it.

 **Which is §21's own principle turned on the companion.** Each index is stated in some language, and
 an index whose language has been retired cannot be repaired by working harder in it. **The four
 vocabularies are the language; V1–V7 was the coordinate system that failed.**

### 14.5.6 What the second operator localises, and what it leaves undetermined

### 14.5.7 The seed is constructible, and it is a size rather than a set

### 14.5.8 The seed is linear in dimension, and the coefficient was in the bibliography

 §14.5.7 measures the seed on scattered shapes. On a controlled family it has a law.

  family                 seed at d = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6        law
  full box 3ᵈ            4 · 6 · 8 · 10 · 12              **2d**
  full box 4ᵈ            6 · 9 · 12 · 15 · 18             **3d**
  down-set, c = 4        5 · 6 · 7 · 8                    **d + 3**
  down-set, c = 5        6 · 7 · 8 · 9                    **d + 4**

    **The seed is LINEAR in dimension and the index is not.** Compression is |X| over a
    linear term, which is why Λ₈ compresses 89× and Janet, at d = 2, compresses 3×.

 **And Λ does NOT fit it** — a claim this section carried until §14.5.9's heuristic correction.
 Under greedy set cover:

  stage    cells    d + c − 1    **set cover**
  Λ₈         976        11           **7**
  Λ₉       1,654        12           **9**
  Λ₁₀      2,535        13           **9**

 **Λ seeds well below the down-set law, and Λ₉ and Λ₁₀ seed identically** — so the seed does not even
 rise with every stage. *This section previously read "it fits Λ on the nose, seed(Λ₈) = 11 = 8 + 3",
 which was prune-greedy's arithmetic.* **The law holds for pure down-sets, where it is exact by
 branch and bound; Λ is more constrained than a down-set and seeds more cheaply.** Register 511.

 **The coefficient was already in this book's References, glossed and left.** The Carathéodory entry
 reads *for a semilattice with subsemilattices as convex sets it is the **breadth**, and the Helly
 number is the height* — and **the breadth of a product of d chains is d.**

    **seed = Carathéodory number + alphabet cost.**

 **Which is why the seed cannot be constant.** A generating set must reach the breadth of what it
 generates, and the breadth of a d-dimensional product is d; anything smaller misses a coordinate.
 The alphabet cost is the remainder — one witness per value no envelope step already supplies.

 before measuring, on four indexes:

  the register index      3      32    7          7          5
  the reference index     4      60    0          7          6
  the bibliography index  4      52    0          7          6

 **Only the first row is a genuine test.** The audit index is rebuilt from this book's own printed
 table and the prediction is **exact**. The other three are reconstructions — the register classifier
 used here gives 32 cells and E = 7 where §28.9 gives 33 and 6, and the reference and bibliography
 indexes were rebuilt from their coordinate names with constraints supplied for the purpose. **Those
 rows test the formula on shapes invented for it.**

    **So: one exact prediction on a real object, and agreement within one on three
    synthetic ones. The Carathéodory term is exact — a generating set cannot fall below
    the breadth of what it generates. The alphabet term OVER-ESTIMATES**, because a
    single witness often covers a value some envelope step has already supplied.

 Register 495.

 **And tested up the tower it is exact three times and then breaks, and the break is the dichotomy.**

  stage    d      cells   predicted   measured   the axis it added
  Λ₈       8        976       11         **11**   —
  Λ₉       9      1,654       12         **12**   2S′, a COUNTING axis
  Λ₁₀     10      2,535       13         **13**   v, a COUNTING axis
  **Λ₁₁**  11     13,585       16         **18**   2J_c, the first COUPLING axis

 and 9, and the counting/coupling split they were read as showing is withdrawn with register 497.*

    **A counting axis costs the seed one cell. A coupling axis costs five.**

 — is the same statement read through the seed. **`d + (largest alphabet − 1)` is a counting-axis
 formula**, and it fails at precisely the stage where the tower stops counting and starts coupling.

 further coupling axes above Λ₁₁ it is nearer **twenty-eight**, still 7,000× against 199,130 cells,
 but reached by the right half of the dichotomy. Register 496.

  new axis                        parents   alphabet   cells   seed cost
  counting  y ≤ x₃                    1         4        56       **+1**
  counting  y ≤ x₀                    1         4       119       **+2**
  counting  y free                    1         4       140       **+2**
  coupling  |y − x₀| ≤ x₁             **2**     7       161      **+10**

  2 · 7                   10–11

4748	## 17. Extension — cells, axes, constraints
  4749	    A closed index determines what may be added to it.
  4750	
  4751	 Three operations, and only three: change the cells, change the axes, change the constraints.
  4752	
  4753	### 17.1 E1 — which cells may be added
  4754	    Λ ∪ {x} is closed iff for every y ∈ Λ, both x∨y and x∧y lie in Λ ∪ {x}
  4755	
  4756	 **100% over 288 tests.** A cell may be added exactly when it sits in a hole whose joins and meets fall back into the lattice.
  4757	
  4758	### 17.2 E2 — which axes may be adjoined
  4759	    Λ × h is closed iff h is a lattice homomorphism
  4760	
  4761	 **100% over 424 tests.** Projections, maxima, minima and constants qualify; sums, products and differences do not.
  4762	
  4763	 **And a theorem in the other direction:**
  4764	
  4765	    Theorem 10.1 (adjunction never repairs). For any h : S → H, with S′ = {(x, h(x))}: S′ closed ⇒ S
  4766	    closed. Proof. For x, y ∈ S, the join of (x,h(x)) and (y,h(y)) is (x∨y, h(x)∨h(y)). If S′ is closed this lies
  4767	    in S′, so x∨y ∈ S. Meets likewise. ∎ Contrapositive: a non-closed set cannot be repaired by
  4768	    adjoining any function of its coordinates. Tested on seven functions including the identity and a
  4769	    constant; none repairs.
  4770	
  4771	 **Three repair routes remain**, and only three: **enlarge** (add cells), **restrict** (remove cells), **reorder** (change neither). The calendar of Chapter 6 is repaired by reordering, at a cost of usability.

## 17. Extension — cells, axes, constraints
    A closed index determines what may be added to it.

 Three operations, and only three: change the cells, change the axes, change the constraints.

### 17.1 E1 — which cells may be added
    Λ ∪ {x} is closed iff for every y ∈ Λ, both x∨y and x∧y lie in Λ ∪ {x}

 **100% over 288 tests.** A cell may be added exactly when it sits in a hole whose joins and meets fall back into the lattice.

### 17.2 E2 — which axes may be adjoined
    Λ × h is closed iff h is a lattice homomorphism

 **100% over 424 tests.** Projections, maxima, minima and constants qualify; sums, products and differences do not.

 **And a theorem in the other direction:**

    Theorem 10.1 (adjunction never repairs). For any h : S → H, with S′ = {(x, h(x))}: S′ closed ⇒ S
    closed. Proof. For x, y ∈ S, the join of (x,h(x)) and (y,h(y)) is (x∨y, h(x)∨h(y)). If S′ is closed this lies
    in S′, so x∨y ∈ S. Meets likewise. ∎ Contrapositive: a non-closed set cannot be repaired by
    adjoining any function of its coordinates. Tested on seven functions including the identity and a
    constant; none repairs.

 **Three repair routes remain**, and only three: **enlarge** (add cells), **restrict** (remove cells), **reorder** (change neither). The calendar of Chapter 6 is repaired by reordering, at a cost of usability.

 **The method has no domain at *p* = 1.** It is the only hard singularity in the structure; every other limit is a threshold with data on both sides.

### 18.6 E(X) is the prediction budget
 The five limitations above add up to something the book can now state in one line, and it
 answers the question this work began with.

 A prediction is a claim that a cell exists which the index does not carry. The only cells an index
 can propose are those its own structure admits and its extension denies — and that set is exactly ℛ(X)
 ∖ X.

    The number of predictions an index can make is E(X).

### 18.6.1 What that means for the five indices this book keeps

| index | E(X) | predictions available | and they are |
|---|---|---|---|
| the periodic table | 36 | 36 | **all impossible** |
| the calendar | 7 | 7 | **all impossible** |
| a subnet with a hole | 8 | 8 | **all impossible** |
| **the box ordering, and Λ** | **0** | **0** | — |
| **the bibliography** | **6** | **6** | **all occupiable — two already named** |

 **Every prediction the first three can make is wrong.** Period-1 group-2 and its thirty-five kin. The thirty-first of February and its six. Λ can propose nothing at all. **The fifth row is the exception, and it is the only place in this book where a prediction is both available and true.**

 **The bibliography, indexed on era, retrieval redundancy ρ, access and depth of entry, holds twenty-two sources over seven cells and admits six it does not carry.** Under exhaustive relabelling E falls from six to two and never to zero, so by §16.7.1 it is irreducible in the same sense as the asteroid belt and unlike the periodic table, whose thirty-six vanish under Janet. **The two survivors are a born-digital literature at ρ ≥ 4 read only in abstract, and a digitised pre-digital source read in full and entered once.** Both are occupiable and both name a route, which is exactly what the belt's absences do not: resonance strength enters at *e*^|p−q|, so the belt's empty cells are empty because nothing can sit in them.

    Closure abolishes prediction. It does not abolish the bibliography,
    because a bibliography is never closed — E(search) > 0 always, by §29.1,
    and the cells it admits are documents that exist.

 **Which gives §16.7.1 a third verdict it did not have.** That section sorts a defect into *an artefact of the layout*, removable by re-coordinatisation, and *a fact about the world*, surviving every one. The bibliography is the second kind and its cells are still fillable, so the two verdicts are not exhaustive:

| the defect | reaches zero? | its predictions |
|---|---|---|
| the periodic table | **yes**, under Janet | impossible — the layout's fault |
| the asteroid belt | **no**, 2 → 1 | impossible — nothing can occupy them |
| **the bibliography** | **no**, 6 → 2 | **possible, and unfilled** |

 **Irreducible does not mean unoccupiable.** An index can carry a defect no re-coordinatisation removes whose cells are nevertheless real and empty for want of work — and that is the only shape in which this method predicts anything.

### 18.6.2 And it is forced, not observed
 Two results already in this part combine to give it.

 **E(X) = 0** says there is no missing **cell** to propose. **Theorem 11.2** says there is no hidden **quantity** to derive.

 Together:

    A fully defined index has nothing left to say.

 **That is the whole answer to whether Λ is predictive.** Not that it is a weak predictor. Not that it wants more coordinates. **There is no gap in it for a prediction to occupy.**

### 18.6.3 Where prediction actually lives
 Λ indexes cells. It does not index values.

 The Sc VI 6s cell of §25.6 is in Λ — its coordinates are ordinary integers, and the lattice admits it without comment. **Its energy is not**, and no closure property supplies it.

| | |
|---|---|
| **the cell** | indexed, E = 0, nothing to predict |
| **the value** | not indexed, and therefore predictable |

 **δ is precisely the value's departure from what the index determines.**

    Prediction requires an incompleteness, and a complete index has none.

 **Which is why the bracket must be handed two measured neighbours before it can say anything at all.** It is not extracting a prediction from the lattice. **It is carrying a constraint between two measurements the lattice never had.**

### 18.6.4 The trade, stated plainly
 An index may be complete or it may be predictive. It cannot be both.

 **Not because completeness is dull**, but because a prediction is a proposal about an unlisted cell, and completeness is the property of having no unlisted cells. The periodic table can propose thirty-six things because it is incomplete. **Λ can propose nothing because it is not.**

 **This is the fifth and largest of the negatives**, and everything else in this part is a special case of it.

### 18.7 Why the negatives are the contribution
 Λ is a bijective recoding of existing quantum numbers. It adds no physics. A reader will observe this within
 a page, and they will be right.

 **That is the point.** A recoding that adds nothing and still exhibits closure, self-reference, self-defence and these five limitations is demonstrating a property of **indexing**, not of atoms. If Λ contained new physics the results would be about atoms and worth much less.

## 19. Retrieval as a lattice problem

### Closure (Ch. 14)
`X` is closed iff `X = ℛ(X)`. **This is Bergman's double-projection theorem** specialised to
products of chains, itself a consequence of **Baker–Pixley (1975)** for any algebra with a majority
term. E(X)=0 is *global consistency* of a binary constraint network — **Montanari 1974**,
**Dechter 1992** (the book had been citing **Freuder 1982** for Dechter's theorem; corrected at
R 400). The constraint class is a **staircase** constraint (Deville, Barták & Van Hentenryck 1999).
So **E(Λ)=0 is the discovery that Λ is a sublattice**, and sublattices have been binary-determined
since 1975. ℛ is extensive, monotone, idempotent — 150/150. The book claims no novelty for the
machinery; the application is computing the closure defect *of an index*.

**Scope:** each coordinate must be presented as a chain. Bundling two chains into one non-chain
coordinate hides structure from ℛ.

**The seed.** No cell of Λ is removable — ℛ(Λ\\{x}) = Λ for all 976. **seed(Λ₈) = 7, exact by
branch and bound** — a compression of 139:1. Prune-greedy said 10–13 for twelve cycles and every
law fitted to its output was fitted to its failures (§14.5.9; the protocol §2.24 *never one
heuristic* is what that earned). Laws now exact: a down-set seeds at d+c−1, a full box at d+c−2.
**seed = Carathéodory number + alphabet cost**, and the breadth of a product of d chains is d.
Every one of 219 minimum covers contains an s→s, s→p, p→s, p→p, a NULL (q=0) and a FULL (q=k)
transition — **the constraint is on the channel, not the cell.**

**The family of closed indexes is open.** Every member has E=0; the family is closed under
intersection, not union; **E(Cl(U)) = 2^|U| − |Cl(U)|**, i.e. ℛ(Cl(U)) is the entire power set.

- **E1 cells:** `Λ ∪ {x}` closed iff for every y, both x∨y and x∧y land in Λ ∪ {x}. 100%/288.

**Part III is read whole — Chapters 14, 17 and 18, §18.4.1 included. Registered as 1658 (1,453 entries), gates pass, banked at `2_6l`, digest extended to 1,855 words.**

**It settles the legality of what we did to Λ_spectra.** §18.4.1 admits four operations — relabel a coordinate's values, re-coordinatise the same content, refine a fibration, drop a coordinate. Moving the Z bound from 118 to 120 is the *first* of them: an alphabet relabelled, no coordinate added. That's why E didn't move, and the register can now say so from the law rather than from the computation happening to agree.

**And Theorem 10.1 makes the four earlier failures structural rather than unlucky.** *Adjunction never repairs* — a non-closed set cannot be closed by adjoining **any** function of its coordinates, tested on seven including the identity and a constant. R 1581, 1599, 1602 and 1608 weren't four attempts that happened to fail; they were four attempts at an operation the book proves cannot work.

Three things bear directly on the build: E3's criterion is that admissibility belongs to the *pair* (h, q) and that **only the join can break a bound** — so our two rules are safe by inspection exactly as Λ's seven are, each reading one coordinate over a chain, and none summing. §17.4's repair is the one we may need later: a sum bound can't be imposed, but a sum can be **indexed**, at the price of making comparable some pairs that were incomparable. And §18.6 — the number of predictions an index can make is E(X) — puts prediction in the **value**, never the cell, which is precisely what the Ga I finding was about.

Now the honest part, because the alternative is the fault this project exists to catch. **I cannot read the remaining ~150,000 words in this session's context.** What's left: Part II (the construction of Λ), Chapters 15, 16 and 19, Parts IV–VII including the Löwdin challenge, every appendix, and the bodies of all four compendia. If I kept going I'd start skimming and calling it reading, and the register would carry a claim about text nobody has read — §2.20's own exception clause says a source consulted at half length is a different source.

`DIGEST.md` names each unread part explicitly so the gap can't close over quietly, and it's structured so a fresh session resumes from it rather than from nothing. My recommendation for the next pass, in order of what governs the rest: **Part II (Ch. 6–13)**, then **Ch. 15–16** (self-reference and self-defence — the six defences and the five failures where the index passed and the physics didn't), then the compendium bodies.

input.file_text:
# THE HANDOFF PROTOCOL — §H
**A session is a container that will die. The protocol is what survives it.**

Adopted session 1.8, 2026-08-15, at M's instruction: *this need is becoming more common as the
work expands.* Referenced hereafter as **§H**, with clauses **§H.1** to **§H.9**.

This is a protocol in the sense of Part I §2 — procedural, not a theorem. It is written to be
**run and checked**, not read and agreed with. Its test is §H.8: a handoff that has not produced
a passing certificate has not happened, whatever was written.

---

## §H.0 What a handoff is for

A new session begins with no memory of the last one. What it has is: whatever files it is given,
whatever the register says, and whatever a bridge document tells it. **Everything else is lost**,
including every intention that was held in the head of the outgoing session and never written.

The failure mode is not losing files. It is losing **why** — which thread was open, which decision
was M's and still unmade, which number is provisional, which claim was checked and which was
merely written. A file survives; a context does not, unless it is made into a file.

> **The handoff is complete when the incoming session can do the next piece of work without
> asking a question the outgoing session could have answered.**

---

## §H.1 The four things that must transfer

| | what | where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **The work** — every data file, script, artefact, capture | the bank archive |
| **2** | **The record** — the register, complete and rebuilt | `REGISTER.md`, `REGISTER-DATA.md` |
| **3** | **The orientation** — what a session must hold before it works | `DIGEST.md` |
| **4** | **The state** — open threads, pending decisions, what is provisional | the bridge document |

**All four or none.** Three of four is the dangerous case, because it looks like a handoff.

---

## §H.2 The bridge document

One file, named `BRIDGE-<from>-to-<to>.md`, carrying **eight sections and in this order**:

1. **Identification** — session names, date, project folder, and the transcript filenames.
2. **What this session did** — in register-entry ranges, not prose summary. `R 1642–1658`.
3. **The state of the object** — the live counts, from instruments, with the command that produced
   them. Never recited.
4. **Open threads** — each with: what it is, what has been tried, what would settle it, and
   **whose decision it is**. A thread with no named owner is not an open thread; it is a wish.
5. **Provisional figures** — every number in the record that is a choice rather than a
   measurement, named as such. (§H.6.)
6. **What is read and what is not** — for every document the project holds. Named, not glossed.
7. **The resumption order** — what to do first, second, third, and why that order.
8. **The standing carry-overs** — items older than this session that remain open.

---

## §H.3 The transcripts travel

Transcripts are the only record of *how* a conclusion was reached. The register carries the
conclusion; the transcript carries the reasoning, the failed attempt, and the thing M said in
passing that turned out to matter.

**Copy them into the work tree** — `work/transcripts/` — with the journal that indexes them.
A transcript left in a mount that the next container may not have is not transferred.

---

## §H.4 Nothing is summarised that can be carried

A summary is a lossy compression chosen by the outgoing session, which does not know what the
incoming session will need. **Prefer the artefact to the account of the artefact.** Summarise only
what cannot travel: a decision's reasoning, a discarded route, the shape of a conversation.

Corollary: **do not rewrite history to match the present.** Where a document states a figure that
was true when written and is now superseded, leave it and say so in the bridge. R 1656 left three
occurrences of a stale cell count standing because they sat inside historical statements.

---

## §H.5 The bank is the unit of transfer

One archive, everything in it, verified after building rather than before:

```
rm -rf .zeno __pycache__
tar czf /mnt/user-data/outputs/<name>.tar.gz --exclude='.zeno' --exclude='__pycache__' .
tar tzf /mnt/user-data/outputs/<name>.tar.gz | wc -l     # count what actually went in
```

**A bank that has not been listed after building has not been verified.** The count is compared
against the working tree's own count; a mismatch is a finding, not a rounding error.

---

## §H.6 Provisional figures are named

Every number in the record is one of three things, and the bridge says which:
- **measured** — from an instrument, on data, reproducible by rerunning it;
- **chosen** — a statistic, a cap, a bound, a convention. Defensible, and not the only answer;
- **inherited** — carried from earlier work and not re-derived in this session.

The second kind is the one that causes damage, because it reads as the first. Ga I's δ = 1.31599
is a **median** where the same members give a mean of 1.2949 — one dataset, two statistics, and
nothing in the cell says so. Z = 120 is a **chosen** bound; E = 0 holds at any.

---

## §H.7 The incoming session's first four acts

Written for the reader of the bridge, in order:

1. **Read `DIGEST.md`.** It holds the one claim, the objects, the generating rules, §18.4.1's
   admitted operations, the gates, and what is read and unread.
2. **Read the bridge.** Open threads and pending decisions.
3. **Run both gates before touching anything** — `The_Method_1_6_audits.py` (25) and
   `roundtrip.py` (5/5). A session that begins by changing something has no baseline to compare to.
4. **Rebuild the register** and confirm the entry count matches what the bridge states.

---

## §H.8 The handoff certificate

A handoff is complete when **all seven** return true. This is checkable, and §4.6 requires that a
check be capable of failing before its passing is evidence — each clause below can fail.

| | clause | how it fails |
|---|---|---|
| **C1** | both gates pass in the outgoing session | an audit or a round-trip is red |
| **C2** | the register rebuilds and its count is stated | `register_gen.py` errors, or the count is recited rather than read |
| **C3** | every generated artefact regenerates identically | a compendium is stale — the R 1655 failure |
| **C4** | the bank lists at the expected file count | files excluded by a stray pattern |
| **C5** | transcripts and journal are inside the bank | left in a mount |
| **C6** | the bridge names every open thread with an owner | a thread with no owner |
| **C7** | the bridge names what is unread | a gap that closes over quietly |

**Certificate form.** Print the seven with their evidence. §18.4.1's practice applies: the
certificate is *exhibited, never found*, and what is falsifiable is the exhibition.

---

## §H.9 What this protocol does not do

It does not preserve judgement. The incoming session will not hold what the outgoing one
understood; it will hold what was written. **Write the disagreement, not only the conclusion** —
where M corrected a direction, the correction is the content and the conclusion is the residue.

And it does not make a handoff free. It makes it **bounded**: the cost is one bridge, one archive
listing, and one certificate, paid once at the end of a session rather than continuously in
recovered ground at the start of the next.

> A session that ends without a certificate has not ended. It has merely stopped.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""§H.8 — the handoff certificate. Seven clauses, each capable of failing.

Usage:  python3 handoff_cert.py <bank.tar.gz> <bridge.md>
Prints the seven with evidence and exits non-zero if any fails.
"""
import csv, os, re, subprocess, sys, tarfile

WORK = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
BANK = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else None
BRIDGE = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None
res = []

def clause(cid, name, ok, evidence):
    res.append((cid, name, ok, evidence))

# C1 — both gates pass
def run(script):
    p = subprocess.run(['timeout', '900', 'python3', script], cwd=WORK,
                       capture_output=True, text=True)
    return p.stdout + p.stderr
try:
    a = run('The_Method_1_6_audits.py'); r = run('roundtrip.py')
    ok = ('ALL TWENTY-FIVE PASS' in a) and ('5 of 5 round-trip' in r)
    n_fail = r.count('FAIL')
    clause('C1', 'both gates pass', ok,
           f"audits: {'ALL TWENTY-FIVE PASS' if 'ALL TWENTY-FIVE PASS' in a else 'NOT CLEAN'} · "
           f"round-trip: {'5 of 5' if '5 of 5 round-trip' in r else f'{n_fail} FAIL'}")
except Exception as e:
    clause('C1', 'both gates pass', False, f'gate run errored: {e}')

# C2 — register rebuilds, count read not recited
try:
    p = subprocess.run(['timeout', '900', 'python3', 'register_gen.py'], cwd=WORK,
                       capture_output=True, text=True)
    m = re.search(r'([0-9,]+) entries', p.stdout)
    held = open(os.path.join(WORK, 'REGISTER.md'), encoding='utf-8').read()
    mh = re.search(r'([0-9,]+) entries', held)
    ok = bool(m and mh and m.group(1) == mh.group(1)) and p.returncode == 0
    clause('C2', 'register rebuilds; count read from it', ok,
           f"generated {m.group(1) if m else '?'} · held {mh.group(1) if mh else '?'}")
except Exception as e:
    clause('C2', 'register rebuilds; count read from it', False, str(e))

# C3 — generated artefacts regenerate identically (round-trip already tests it; report per file)
try:
    r = run('roundtrip.py')
    per = re.findall(r'(\S+\.md)\s+(PASS|FAIL)', r)
    ok = all(v == 'PASS' for _, v in per) and len(per) >= 5
    clause('C3', 'every generated artefact regenerates', ok,
           ' · '.join(f'{k} {v}' for k, v in per) or 'no artefacts reported')
except Exception as e:
    clause('C3', 'every generated artefact regenerates', False, str(e))

# C4 — the bank lists at the expected file count
try:
    tree = sum(1 for root, dirs, files in os.walk(WORK)
               for f in files
               if '.zeno' not in root and '__pycache__' not in root)
    if BANK and os.path.exists(BANK):
        with tarfile.open(BANK) as t:
            inbank = sum(1 for m in t.getmembers() if m.isfile())
        ok = inbank >= tree
        clause('C4', 'bank lists at the tree count', ok,
               f'tree {tree} files · bank {inbank} files')
    else:
        clause('C4', 'bank lists at the tree count', False, f'bank not found: {BANK}')
except Exception as e:
    clause('C4', 'bank lists at the tree count', False, str(e))

# C5 — transcripts and journal inside the bank
try:
    if BANK and os.path.exists(BANK):
        with tarfile.open(BANK) as t:
            names = t.getnames()
        tx = [n for n in names if '/transcripts/' in n or n.startswith('./transcripts/')]
        has_journal = any(n.endswith('journal.txt') for n in tx)
        ok = len(tx) >= 2 and has_journal
        clause('C5', 'transcripts and journal in the bank', ok,
               f'{len([n for n in tx if n.endswith(".txt")])} files, journal {"yes" if has_journal else "NO"}')
    else:
        clause('C5', 'transcripts and journal in the bank', False, 'no bank')
except Exception as e:
    clause('C5', 'transcripts and journal in the bank', False, str(e))

# C6 — the bridge names every open thread with an owner
try:
    b = open(BRIDGE, encoding='utf-8').read() if BRIDGE else ''
    threads = re.findall(r'\*\*T(\d+)\s*·\s*(.+?)\.\s*Owner:\s*(.+?)\.\*\*', b)
    ok = len(threads) > 0 and all(o.strip() for _, _, o in threads)
    clause('C6', 'open threads carry owners', ok,
           ' · '.join(f'T{n} → {o.strip()}' for n, _, o in threads) or 'none found')
except Exception as e:
    clause('C6', 'open threads carry owners', False, str(e))

# C7 — the bridge names what is unread
try:
    b = open(BRIDGE, encoding='utf-8').read() if BRIDGE else ''
    d = open(os.path.join(WORK, 'DIGEST.md'), encoding='utf-8').read()
    ok = ('Unread' in b or 'unread' in b) and ('NOT READ' in d or 'not read' in d or 'Unread' in d)
    clause('C7', 'the unread is named', ok,
           f"bridge {'names it' if 'nread' in b else 'SILENT'} · digest {'names it' if 'ot read' in d.lower() or 'nread' in d else 'SILENT'}")
except Exception as e:
    clause('C7', 'the unread is named', False, str(e))

print('=== §H.8 HANDOFF CERTIFICATE ===')
for cid, name, ok, ev in res:
    print(f'  {cid}  {"PASS" if ok else "FAIL"}  {name}')
    print(f'        {ev}')
passed = sum(1 for *_, ok, _ in [(c, n, o, e) for c, n, o, e in res] if ok)
print(f'\n{passed} of {len(res)} clauses pass')
if passed != len(res):
    print('HANDOFF INCOMPLETE — a session that ends without a certificate has not ended.')
    sys.exit(1)
print('HANDOFF COMPLETE.')

    d = open(os.path.join(WORK, 'DIGEST.md'), encoding='utf-8').read()
    ok = ('Unread' in b or 'unread' in b) and ('NOT READ' in d or 'not read' in d or 'Unread' in d)
    clause('C7', 'the unread is named', ok,
